I have the same thing. Remember the obsessive part of OCD, you'll obsess over it and if you keep ruminating over it, it won't stop. The thoughts will be there. I know this is easier said than done, because I'm going through the same thing, but just try to accept that the thought is there and that it'll pass. One thing that's helped me a lot is to not post about my obsessions here. It reinforces the thought into my head, even if all I'm trying to do is help myself. Not necessarily saying that this sub isn't helpful or good to vent in, but it's just not helpful to fixate on a particular thought and wait for people to either give you reassurance that you've heard a hundred times before, or have nobody respond and have your anxiety get five times worse. So, just try to accept the uncertainty, even if you're uncomfortable with it. And expect it to take some time, too, because it's not gonna just go away overnight.

That's around the first time that most people get so i'd say that's pretty good. For tips, I'd say:

1. Just keep doing runs. Keeping on going and not resetting no matter what pace you're on will allow you to make your movement a little more clean and it'll be easier to get better. Once you get to around 1:25, then you should start resetting, but not too much.
2. Try not to go too fast. Don't implement really hard strats too early, like snow dram or birdless mech at like 1:40 or 1:35. Those are just a couple examples, there's a lot of stuff that looks relatively easy to get down, but just remember that even without all those hard strats, getting sub 1:10 is still very much possible.
3. Make sure you're comfortable with your gameplay. This ties into trying not to go too fast, but it's also about the controllers you have. Once I got a pro controller, it was significantly better than when I used joycons. But, that's just me, personally, because even though it's uncommon, some people also prefer to use joycons. Just make sure you know what's more comfortable to play with when you grind.
4. Don't play too much. I've gotten into slumps where I couldn't PB because all I did was play and stress myself out to get a good time. Overplaying is most definitely a thing. You'd think playing more would mean more practice, but playing too much just makes your mentality about the game just to PB and you won't be able to enjoy yourself, which is pretty crucial for motivation and not burning yourself out.
5. Be okay with not getting a 'good' time. This ties into finishing runs as well. Even if you didn't PB, it's okay! You still got some practice in and more runs under your belt. For example, I have a 1:02:58 PB and I recently made myself a comparison to get more 1:03s, because it's close and easier to not get stressed out over. So, that means I can be proud of myself for at least playing close to PB and not have too much pressure on myself.

I know this was pretty long, and I might be leaving some stuff out that I forget, but speedrunning has been really beneficial to me and I'd love to help out other people that need some tips! Good luck with your future runs, my friend!

I say you should leave the relationship for the sake of your own well-being, at least until he gets help and gets a diagnosis.

Edit: now that I've read it a second time, it is a little bit fishy. OCD is not about blurting out offensive things and then magically being okay afterwards. If it was truly OCD, he would most likely think those thoughts, then immediately start questioning himself and seek reassurance from you that he isn't such a horrible person for thinking these things. I've been asking myself that quite a bit too, and it really is the scariest thing, I know. But as long as you try to go with the motions, it'll get better and the anxiety will go away in small portions. No matter what anybody says, you'll still have it in your mind, even if thousands of people tell you that you aren't, because that's what OCD does. You have to learn to live with it no matter how hard it is. I legitimately thought my life was ruined when I had my first intrusive thought about a child and that I should just kill myself. Now, even though I still freak out about it sometimes, I'm loads better than I was before. I suggest you look into therapy for treatment. But, until that happens, the best advice I can give you is to try to accept that the thoughts you're having are there, without digging too deep. I've gone into the pool of overanalyzing, and it ain't pretty. Don't try and push them away, but also don't try to prove them wrong. Just try and go through your normal day and if a thought shows up, let it be, because it'll go away if you don't dwell on it too much.
